title: The Line That Arrived in Two Pieces: Reading Lines From a Device That Gives You Whatever It Has

questions.question: A serial port's readyRead fires and readAll() returns "temp 21". What is that?
options: Whatever had arrived: possibly the start of a line, to be joined to the next chunk
A line that is missing its newline and should be dropped
questions.explanation: A chunk is not a line: the cut falls wherever the arrival did.

questions.question: Why does the test cut the same bytes 629 ways?
options: Because a device can cut a message anywhere, and the lines must come out the same each time
questions.explanation: Cutting at every position and into three chunks finds a bug that only some cuts show.

questions.question: What does "a\r\nb".split('\n').at(0) give?
options: a followed by a carriage return, 2 bytes
questions.explanation: Splitting at \n alone leaves the \r on the line.

questions.question: Why is a line over the limit dropped and not just truncated?
options: A truncated line looks like a valid shorter line, and the rest of it would become the next one
questions.explanation: The assembler skips to the newline that ends it and counts it.

questions.question: 100000 bytes of noise with no newline arrive. How many does the assembler hold?
options: None: it passed the limit, stopped keeping them and is skipping until a newline
questions.explanation: Its memory is bounded by the limit however much noise arrives.

questions.question: A device sends half a line and stops. What does the assembler do?
options: Returns the half line after a timeout
Holds it: it has no timeout, and a caller that needs one must add it
questions.explanation: Not timing out a stalled line is stated in what the lesson does not do.
